narrative:
The model estimated a 57% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above half, the law school treated your application as too risky and denied admission.

The most important factor was your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. This was the dominant reason the prediction leaned toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 31, below the accepted-student average of about 37. In your individual case, however, this factor pulled toward passing rather than failure. The third most important factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, also below the accepted-student average of 3.23; it too modestly supported passing. Even so, the very low third-year standing outweighed those two supportive signals and drove the denial.

To improve your chances, focus first on raising your academic standing in advanced coursework and seek advising about whether to delay reapplication until your record improves. You should also consider retaking the LSAT and taking steps to strengthen your undergraduate academic profile, then reapply once you can show a clearer upward trend and a lower predicted bar-exam risk.
